title: Merge Intervals — Collapsing Overlapping Ranges
summary: Collapsing a list of ranges into their disjoint union in one linear pass — the entry point for every interval question, and the pattern that every other topic in this group builds on.

slides.markdown:
Give someone a pile of ranges — meeting times, IP blocks, date spans — and ask for their **disjoint union**: the fewest ranges that cover exactly the same ground with no overlaps. That's Merge Intervals, and it's the gateway problem for an entire family of interval questions.

The trick that makes it easy: **sort by start time first.** Once the list is ordered, one linear pass is enough — no nested loops, no re-scanning. Every other topic in this group (insertion, intersection, room counting, sweep line, skyline) reuses this same "sort, then one disciplined pass" shape.

Get this one cold, because interviewers use it to gate whether you can even attempt the harder variants.

slides.sectionTitle: Why sorting first is the whole trick
slides.markdown:
Unsorted, you'd need to compare every interval against every other one to know if it overlaps anything — that's O(n²) territory, and worse, an interval's overlap partner might not even be adjacent in the input order.

Sort by **start** time and something powerful falls out: once you've processed intervals up to index i, the only interval that can possibly extend your current merged range is the *next* one in sorted order. Nothing later can overlap without also overlapping something you've already seen, because starts only increase.

That collapses the problem to a single **left-to-right scan with one running "current merge"** — no backtracking, no re-checking earlier intervals. The sort does the hard work; the pass itself is almost mechanical.

slides.subTitle: The one decision made on every step
slides.markdown:
After sorting, walk the intervals left to right holding one **current merge** — `[start, end]`. For each next interval, there are exactly two outcomes:

- Its start is `<=` the current merge's end → it **overlaps**. Extend the current merge's end to the max of the two ends.
- Its start is `>` the current merge's end → it's **disjoint**. Push the current merge to the result and start a new one from this interval.

Every interval in the list triggers exactly one of those two branches. There's no third case, which is what makes the pass so mechanical once the input is sorted.

<<< Image: a horizontal timeline with 6 intervals drawn as bars at increasing start positions; the first three bars overlap and are shown collapsing into one wider highlighted bar labelled "current merge", then a gap, then two more overlapping bars collapsing into a second highlighted bar — arrows show the scan moving left to right and a small decision diamond at each new bar labelled "start <= current end?" >>>

```python
def merge(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])   # sort by start
    result = [intervals[0]]

    for start, end in intervals[1:]:
        last_end = result[-1][1]
        if start <= last_end:              # overlaps current merge
            result[-1][1] = max(last_end, end)
        else:                              # disjoint — close and start new
            result.append([start, end])

    return result
```

Notice `result[-1]` — the comparison is always against the **last merged interval in the output**, never against `intervals[i-1]` from the input. That distinction is the single most common bug in this problem, covered next.

The bug that survives sorted input and still fails: comparing the next interval against `intervals[i-1]` — the **previous input interval** — instead of the **last interval actually placed in the result**.

Those two are usually the same interval, which is exactly why the bug hides in casual testing. They diverge the moment three or more intervals chain together:

`[1,10], [2,3], [4,5]` — after merging `[1,10]` and `[2,3]` into `[1,10]`, the previous *input* interval is `[2,3]`, but the last *merged* interval is `[1,10]`. Comparing `[4,5]` against `[2,3]` wrongly says "disjoint" and emits a spurious extra interval; comparing against `[1,10]` correctly absorbs it.

Always track and compare against `result[-1]`, never the raw input's previous element.

`[1,2]` and `[2,3]` share only the single point 2. Whether that counts as "overlapping" is a **problem-definition choice**, not a universal rule — and it changes your comparison operator.

- If touching intervals **should merge** (common for calendar/range-coverage problems): use `start <= last_end`.
- If touching intervals are **allowed to stay separate** (common when intervals represent half-open ranges like `[start, end)`): use `start < last_end`.

Getting this backwards either merges things that should stay apart, or leaves a needless split where the problem expected one range. Always confirm which convention the prompt uses — real interview prompts state it explicitly, but only if you ask or read closely.

**O(n log n)** overall, and the sort is entirely responsible for it — the merge pass itself is a single O(n) scan with O(1) work per interval.

This matters when the interviewer asks a follow-up: "what if the intervals arrive already sorted?" Then the sort disappears and the whole algorithm drops to **O(n)**. It's a cheap, correct thing to say out loud — it shows you know *where* the log n factor lives rather than reciting "O(n log n)" as one indivisible fact.

Space is O(n) for the output (or O(1) auxiliary if merging in place into a pre-sorted array, aside from the output itself).

Same underlying overlap logic, different starting point:

| | Merge Intervals | Insert Interval |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Unsorted (or arbitrary) list | Already-merged, sorted list, plus one new interval |
| Work | Sort everything, then one pass | No sort needed — one pass suffices |
| Complexity | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| When it applies | Batch of ranges arriving at once | One range added to an existing, maintained set |

The naive way to handle Insert Interval is to append the new interval and re-run Merge Intervals — that works, but throws away the fact that the rest of the list was already sorted, paying an unnecessary O(n log n). The next topic builds the O(n) version that exploits it.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up outside interviews
slides.markdown:
This exact pattern runs in production systems, not just LeetCode:

- **Calendar apps** merge a user's busy blocks across multiple calendars before rendering free/busy views — often thousands of events collapsed in milliseconds.
- **Firewall and CDN configs** merge overlapping IP/CIDR ranges so a routing table doesn't hold redundant, conflicting entries.
- **Log and monitoring systems** merge overlapping time windows of an outage or alert so a dashboard shows one incident instead of five duplicate ones.

In all three, the same shape holds: sort by start, sweep once, extend-or-close. Recognizing "this is a Merge Intervals problem" in a system-design or take-home context is worth as much as knowing the code.

A junior candidate writes the sort-and-scan and stops. A senior candidate notices what the algorithm assumes: it needs the **entire** input up front, because merging is inherently a batch operation — you can't know an interval is "done" until you've seen everything that might still extend it.

That's why streaming or online variants (new intervals arriving continuously) can't reuse this exact algorithm unmodified — they need either periodic re-merging, an interval tree, or Insert Interval applied incrementally (next topic). If an interviewer pushes on "what if intervals keep arriving," naming that batch-vs-incremental distinction is the answer that separates levels.

This batch/incremental split is the organizing idea for the rest of the group.
